en: The *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* (contained in the Later Han Catalogue) states that the initial precepts for a female novice (*śrāmaṇerikā*) are as follows:
One must not kill living beings; one should have compassion for all creatures as one thinks of one's own parents.
My son, extend your compassion to all wriggling creatures as you would to an infant.
What is meant by "not killing"?
It is to guard one's body, speech, and mind.

One does not kill living beings—whether humans or crawling, breathing creatures—with one’s own body; nor does one do so with one’s hands, nor does one incite others to do so. Seeing that a being has been killed, one does not eat it; hearing that it has been killed, one does not eat it; suspecting that it has been killed, one does not eat it; and knowing it was killed specifically for oneself, one does not eat it.

One must not speak words such as "I shall kill," "I shall harm," or "I shall take revenge"; nor should one say, "Death is a joy," "Killing is a joy," "This person is fat," "That person is thin," or "The meat of this person is excellent," or "The meat of that person is meager."
Nor does the mind harbor thoughts such as, "It would be a pleasure to rob, kill, or harm such-and-such a person," or "Such-and-such a beast is fat; such-and-such one is lean.

One regards all sentient beings with compassion as one's own marrow, as one's father, mother, child, or one's own body—equal and without distinction. With universal equanimity and a single mind, one should always be intent upon the Mahāyāna.
This constitutes the initial training in the precepts for a śrāmaṇerī.
The śrāmaṇerī precepts state:
one must not commit theft.
One must not take even a single coin or more, nor grass, leaves, hair, or grain.
One must not take anything unless the owner gives it with their own hand.

One’s mouth shall not speak of taking, one’s mind shall not think of taking, one’s eyes shall not crave sights, one’s ears shall not crave sounds, one’s nose shall not steal fragrances, one’s tongue shall not covet flavors, one’s body shall not lust after clothing, and one’s heart shall not pilfer desires.
To have no attachment to the six sense-faculties and to constantly establish expedient wisdom is called non-stealing.
This is the precept for a śrāmaṇerikā.
The precepts for a śrāmaṇerikā are:
One must not engage in lustful excess.
What is meant by "must not"?
It means that with a single-minded purity, one's body does not engage in lust, one's mouth does not speak of lust, and one's mind does not think of lust.
Maintaining oneself with clarity, one is like the wind in space, having no dependence or attachment.

One does not engage in sexual misconduct with the body, does not look lustfully with the eyes, does not listen lustfully with the ears, does not smell lustfully with the nose, does not speak lustfully with the mouth, and does not harbor desire in the mind.

Contemplate that the four great elements of the body are fundamentally non-existent; when reckoning earth, water, fire, and wind, there is no self, no person, no life-span, and no vital principle. What, then, is there to lust after? What is there to be attached to?
To resolve upon emptiness, signlessness,
and wishlessness— this constitutes the precepts for a śrāmaṇerī.
These are the śrāmaṇerī precepts:
One must not engage in double-tongued speech or harsh words.
One's speech should be composed and steady; what one has not seen, one must not say one saw, and what one has not heard, one must not say one heard.
Upon seeing evil, do not transmit it; upon hearing evil, do not proclaim it. Directly avoid wicked speech and always practice the four immeasurable minds.
There shall be no idle speech; whenever one speaks, one shall speak only of the Path.

One must not discuss worldly matters, nor discourse on the affairs of kings, ministers, officials, or bandits; one should constantly extol the sutras and dharmas and the right precepts of the Bodhisattvas.
To set one's will upon the Mahāyāna, not to engage in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and to practice the four immeasurable minds—
this constitutes the śrāmaṇerikā precepts.
The śrāmaṇerikā precepts are as follows:
One must not drink alcohol;
one must not crave alcohol; one must not taste alcohol.
Alcohol has thirty-six faults: it leads one astray from the Way, ruins the family, endangers the person, and causes the loss of life—all of these arise because of it.
Dragging east and pulling west, holding south and clinging to north;
unable to recite the sutras and disrespectful toward the Triple Gem;
treating teachers and friends with contempt, and unfilial toward one's parents.
With the mind closed and the intellect obstructed, one remains ignorant from lifetime to lifetime;
failing to encounter the Great Way, the mind lacks discernment. Therefore, do not drink alcohol.
One should seek to leave behind the five aggregates, the five desires, and the five hindrances, attain the five supernormal powers, and achieve liberation from the five realms of existence.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The precepts for śrāmaṇerikās are as follows:

one must not carry incense or flowers to perfume or adorn oneself; the five colors may not be used on robes, footwear, or thread; one must not use various jewels to adorn oneself with necklaces; and one must not wear brocade, embroidery, damask, silk gauze, or fine silks.
One must not gaze with frivolous looks; one should wear coarse garments—blue, black, madder-red, or the saffron-colored robe of nirvāṇa—and walk with head bowed.
Desiring to eliminate the six decays, one should take the precepts as one's fragrance.

They seek to recite the profound Dharma as their true treasure, take the thirty-two marks as their necklaces, and obtain the cultivation of the various secondary characteristics as their raiment; they vow that the six supernormal powers shall be unimpeded, and that the six perfections shall guide all beings.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The precepts for śrāmaṇerikās are as follows:
one must not sit upon high beds made of gold or silver.
One must not think of embroidered silks, brocade covers, or precious cords;
one must not instruct others to seek out fine couches, mats, five-colored painted fans, or the finest woolen fly-whisks.
One must not wear armlets or finger rings;
rather, one should have direct faith, precepts, shame, dread of blame, generosity, extensive learning, and wisdom, with a single-minded and focused devotion.
Constantly seeking samādhi as one’s couch, the mind remains unshaken;
taking the natural arising of manifold wisdom as one’s seat-cloth, the seven factors of enlightenment do not waver as the will is fixed upon the path-mind.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The precepts for śrāmaṇerikās are:
one must not listen to the sounds of singing, dancing, music, or the clapping of hands and drumming of cymbals.
One must neither act for oneself nor instruct others to do so.

One should constantly cultivate one's own person, practice the True Dharma in accordance with it, and refrain from deviant conduct. With a single mind, take refuge in the Buddha; recite the sutras and practice the right path as one's dharma-joy, rather than seeking worldly pleasures.
Listening to the sutras and contemplating them, one enters deeply into their great meaning.
Unless one is ill, one must not ride in carriages, on horses, or elephants.

One should instead keep in mind the lightness of body and the attainment of the eight inconceivable supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) as one's vehicle, thereby crossing over and liberating oneself from the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The precepts for śrāmaṇerikās are:
one must not accumulate precious treasures.
One must not take it up with one's own hands, nor teach others to do so.

One should always be single-mindedly diligent, regarding the Way as a treasure, the Sūtras as supreme, and the meaning as wondrous; one should take the understanding of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as the foundation.
Regarding the three liberations, one does not seek after craving or desire.
Wishing to be free from the nine afflictions, one dwells in the Way for a very long time—without end, without limit, and without boundary—and yet remains without any fixed abode.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
The precepts for śrāmaṇerikās are:
one must not eat at the wrong time.

One should always eat at the proper time and not exceed the prescribed measure; after midday has passed, one must not eat again, even if there are sweet and exquisite flavors of infinite variety. One shall ultimately never eat again.
Nor does he teach others to commit [offenses], nor does his mind even entertain such thoughts.
Even if supreme, spontaneous food were to appear, he would not eat it.
If a householder or a king should pass the time after midday, he likewise does not take food, never committing the transgression until death.
He constantly contemplates meditative concentration; although he consumes all manner of food and drink, he takes only what is necessary to sustain his life.
He desires that all beings may understand deeply and fulfill their vows, attaining the ten powers as their sustenance.
These are the precepts for śrāmaṇerikās.
Once a śrāmaṇerikā has received the ten precepts and pursues the Way with pure intent, if she is able to practice these ten matters, the five hundred precepts will naturally be fully realized.

It is, for example, like a person whose head, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, mind, belly, and back are not damaged, whose sense faculties are complete, and who possesses all the intestines, stomach, lungs, liver, five viscera, joints, tendons, and veins.
For example, when the roots of a tree are secure and complete, not withered or decayed, its trunk, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits naturally flourish and grow profusely.

In the same way, a śrāmaṇerikā who can fully prepare the foundation of the ten precepts will find that her five hundred precepts are all completely fulfilled; she may then attain supernormal powers and reach everywhere without obstruction.
It is like a fertile field where the seeds do not rot; when wind and rain come at the proper seasons, the five grains ripen in abundance, and the people attain order.
In the same way, if a śrāmaṇerikā can honor the ten precepts, the five hundred precepts are thereby upheld.
For example, when a sovereign’s moral influence is universally impartial, the myriad people live in peace and security.

It is the same for a śrāmaṇerikā: if she can fully observe the ten precepts, the five hundred precepts will naturally and universally be prepared. It is like when parents are compassionate and harmonious; their children, grandchildren, kinsmen, servants, and laborers will naturally follow their lead.
Furthermore, a śrāmaṇerikā should always revere the Triple Gem and honor her preceptor and upādhyāya a hundred thousand million times more than her own parents.
Parents provide for but one lifetime, whereas the upādhyāya brings about liberation that is infinite and boundless.
Mindful of their reciprocal kindness, they do not commit acts of rebellion or treachery.
They constantly loathe this defiled body as if it were a person confined in prison or fallen into a latrine.
They do not crave the female form, nor do they burn with lust for sensual beauty.
It is like being amidst a great fire, or as if dwelling among bandits.
One should regard all beings with thoughts of them being like one's father, mother, child, or own body.
Constantly feeling shame for one's past conduct and harboring a sense of unease, it was only through this that such a body was obtained.

One should understand that these are fundamentally non-existent, like magical illusions; there is neither male nor female, as these are acquired through habitual conduct. Fundamentally, the five realms of existence do not exist, much less males and females.

Those who seek the Mahāyāna realize that all things are empty—like illusions, transformations, dreams, shadows, echoes, mirages, plantain trees, and echoes from deep mountains—arising only through the conjunction of conditions, fundamentally possessing no inherent reality.

Believe that form is like a shadow, sensation is like a plantain tree, perception is like a wild horse, volitional formations are like bubbles, and consciousness is like an illusion—none of these are the self.
They are compounded by causes and conditions; without conditions, they do not exist. They come alone and go alone, with nothing following them.
For one who seeks the Way,
skillful means and wisdom are their parents;
delighting in the Dharma is their siblings.
Not departing from the profound meaning is one's preceptor;
abiding in loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity while dwelling truthfully in the True Dharma are one's sons and daughters;
and the six perfections are one's companions.
The wisdom of supernormal powers serves as the vehicle;
not transgressing the sūtras and precepts while contemplating the meaning of emptiness serves as the dwelling.
Furthermore, a śrāmaṇerikā must not travel alone.
They should have companions of the same class, whether two or three people.
If there are no śrāmaṇerīs, they should travel together with upāsikās.
Female servants must not sit on the same bed or seat as a mahāśrāmaṇera or a man.
Do not speak falsely.
Furthermore, you must not reside at a neighboring monastery.
Unless you are ill, you must not go back and forth there frequently.
When a donor requests that you read the scriptures, you should do so;
you must not act according to your own whims or teach one another as equals. You should show respect and obedience according to seniority and must not be arrogant or unrestrained.
As you guide and instruct one another, if there are faults or transgressions, you should admonish each other in private and must not speak of them in the midst of the assembly.

If one hears of good, one should see it as good and may proclaim it; if one hears of evil, one should see it as evil and must not spread it about, but may only inform the preceptor and must not speak of it to others.
One should constantly reproach oneself, aspire to share in the sight of good, and examine oneself upon seeing evil, feeling sorrow because others' minds do not reach such heights.
If one becomes a śrāmaṇerikā and seeks an upādhyāyī, she should find one who is intelligent, wise, and compliant with the Dharma, so that she may be able to deliver others life after life.
It is like a boat that is complete, sturdy, and solid, capable of carrying one across to the other shore.
If a teacher is not wise and his conduct does not accord with the Dharma, he is not a Great Teacher.

To take on the role of preceptor is like boarding a ruined ship; while attempting to cross the ocean, it sinks midway, drowning everyone on board, and the teacher perishes along with them, leaving nothing behind.
When one first upholds the Dharma and transmits the sutras and precepts to others, being upright and correct, one becomes a teacher.

Hearing that a Great Master wishes to serve as one's *upādhyāya*, if one was originally a *śrāmaṇerī* and cannot obtain his presence, one may call out his name from afar and pay him homage to take him as a teacher; it need not be a face-to-face meeting. If the mind is near, then one is near; if the mind is distant, then one is distant. Even if the bodies are close together, if the minds are discordant and different, they are separated by hundreds of millions of *li*.
When a śrāmaṇerī travels on a road, she must not walk along the same path or accompany a man; she must not share a room or reside in the same monastery as a man or a śramaṇa.

*Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle.
